claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 1G,I.

claims.claim: Nkx2.2a-driven fluorescence of GFP remained stable after MEP glial exit from the spinal cord.
claims.source: We observed that while nkx2.2a-driven fluorescence of GFP remained stable after MEP glial exit from the spinal cord (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,C), we observed a 2.5 fold-decrease in olig2-driven expression of GFP at these same stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,C.

claims.claim: There is a 2.5 fold-decrease in olig2-driven expression of GFP after MEP glial exit from the spinal cord.
claims.source: We observed that while nkx2.2a-driven fluorescence of GFP remained stable after MEP glial exit from the spinal cord (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,C), we observed a 2.5 fold-decrease in olig2-driven expression of GFP at these same stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C.

claims.claim: The olig2 pMN domain and the nkx2.2a lateral floor plate of the neural tube, which are distinct at 24 hpf, lose their defined separation at approximately 30 hpf and merge to give rise to one mixed domain by 48 hpf.
claims.source: We observed that the olig2 pMN domain and the nkx2.2a lateral floor plate of the neural tube, which are distinct at 24 hpf, lose their defined separation at approximately 30 hpf and merge to give rise to one mixed domain by 48 hpf, a phenomenon that has previously been observed and described during OPC specification (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Kessaris et al., 2001; Kucenas et al., 2008a; Scott et al., 2020; Soula et al., 2001; Tsai et al., 2020; Xiong et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and citations.

claims.claim: At 48 hpf, foxd3+ MEP glia with weak expression of olig2 are observed just ventral to the pMN domain.
claims.source: At 48 hpf, we observed foxd3+ MEP glia with weak expression of olig2, just ventral to the pMN domain (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: At 48 hpf, floor plate foxd3+/nkx2.2a+ MEP glia are observed.
claims.source: In foxd3:mcherry;nkx2.2a:mcerulean embryos, we observed floor plate foxd3+/nkx2.2a+ MEP glia at 48 hpf (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: One foxd3+ cell is detected in the ventral spinal cord per hemi-segment of the zebrafish trunk.
claims.source: In all of our imaging, we always detected one foxd3+ cell in the ventral spinal cord per hemi-segment of the zebrafish trunk (Figure 1B, Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a consistent observation across multiple imaging experiments.

claims.claim: At 48 hpf, olig2+/nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia are observed within the mixed olig2/nkx2.2a domain of the spinal cord.
claims.source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we observed olig2+/nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia within the mixed olig2/nkx2.2a domain of the spinal cord at 48 hpf (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The shape and position of MEP glia next to the central canal of the spinal cord are reminiscent of radial glia.
claims.source: We also observed that the shape and the position of these cells next to the central canal of the spinal cord were reminiscent of radial glia (Figure 2A–C).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on morphology and position, supported by imaging data.

claims.claim: All ventral spinal cord nkx2.2a+ cells examined are GFAP+.
claims.source: We found that all ventral spinal cord nkx2.2a+ cells that we examined were GFAP+ (Figure 2D; Park and Appel, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2D and citation.

claims.claim: MEP glia are generated from lateral floor plate nkx2.2a+/olig2+ radial glial precursors.
claims.source: From these studies, we conclude that MEP glia are generated from lateral floor plate nkx2.2a+/olig2+ radial glial precursors, and maintain expression of both CNS and PNS markers once in the PNS.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claims.claim: MEP glia maintain expression of both CNS and PNS markers once in the PNS.
claims.source: From these studies, we conclude that MEP glia are generated from lateral floor plate nkx2.2a+/olig2+ radial glial precursors, and maintain expression of both CNS and PNS markers once in the PNS.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claims.claim: Foxd3:mcherry heterozygous larvae label foxd3+ MEP glia as well as neural crest-derived cells, including dorsal root ganglia (DRG) and Schwann cells.
claims.source: While foxd3:mcherry heterozygous larvae label foxd3+ MEP glia as well as neural crest-derived cells, including dorsal root ganglia (DRG) and Schwann cells (Figure 1B–C, Figure 2A–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3A), foxd3:mcherry homozygous larvae, which we will refer to as foxd3-/- larvae, lack these neural crest derivatives as well as MEP glia along spinal motor nerve axons (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data.

claims.claim: Foxd3-/- larvae lack neural crest derivatives as well as MEP glia along spinal motor nerve axons.
claims.source: While foxd3:mcherry heterozygous larvae label foxd3+ MEP glia as well as neural crest-derived cells, including dorsal root ganglia (DRG) and Schwann cells (Figure 1B–C, Figure 2A–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3A), foxd3:mcherry homozygous larvae, which we will refer to as foxd3-/- larvae, lack these neural crest derivatives as well as MEP glia along spinal motor nerve axons (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: In foxd3-/- larvae, foxd3+ MEP glia stay in the ventral spinal cord and fail to exit into the periphery.
claims.source: When we time-lapse imaged olig2:egfp;foxd3:mcherry;foxd3+/- and -/- larvae from 48 to 72 hpf, we observed that foxd3+ MEP glia migrated onto peripheral motor nerves in foxd3+/- siblings (Figure 3A and Video 1), while they stayed in the ventral spinal cord and failed to exit into the periphery in mutants (Figure 3A and Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 3A and Videos 1-2.

claims.claim: Spinal cord OPCs develop at the expected developmental stage in foxd3-/- larvae.
claims.source: Because spinal cord OPCs developed at the expected developmental stage (Figure 3A and Video 2) and the morphology and body length of foxd3-/- larvae were comparable to their control siblings (Figure 3B), we ruled out the possibility that failure of MEP glial exit from the spinal cord was the consequence of developmental delay or perturbed neural tube patterning in foxd3-/- larvae.
claims.evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 3A, Video 2, and Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The morphology and body length of foxd3-/- larvae are comparable to their control siblings.
claims.source: Because spinal cord OPCs developed at the expected developmental stage (Figure 3A and Video 2) and the morphology and body length of foxd3-/- larvae were comparable to their control siblings (Figure 3B), we ruled out the possibility that failure of MEP glial exit from the spinal cord was the consequence of developmental delay or perturbed neural tube patterning in foxd3-/- larvae.
claims.evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: By 72 hpf, foxd3+/- siblings have peripheral MEP glia on 100% of their spinal motor nerve roots.
claims.source: By 72 hpf, foxd3+/- siblings had peripheral MEP glia on 100% of their spinal motor nerve roots (Figure 3A,C).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 3A,C.

claims.claim: No MEP glia are observed in the PNS of foxd3-/- larvae at 72 hpf.
claims.source: In contrast, we did not observe any MEP glia in the PNS of foxd3-/- larvae (Figure 3A,C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 3A,C.

claims.claim: Ectopic, peripheral OPCs are observed along motor nerves in foxd3-/- larvae.
claims.source: However, we did observe ectopic, peripheral OPCs along motor nerves in foxd3-/- larvae (Figure 3A,D), which is consistent with the absence of peripheral MEP glia (Fontenas et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 3A,D and citations.

claims.claim: MEP glia are present and can differentiate in the absence of Foxd3.
claims.source: Therefore, we conclude that MEP glia are present and can differentiate in the absence of Foxd3.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from in situ hybridization data showing wif1+ cells in foxd3-/- larvae.

claims.claim: The olig2+/foxd3+ cells observed in the CNS of foxd3-/- larvae are HuC- and therefore not neurons.
claims.source: Analysis of single z-plane confocal images revealed that the olig2+/foxd3+ cells we observed in the CNS of foxd3-/- larvae were HuC-, and therefore, not neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Centrally located MEP glia in foxd3-/- larvae are Sox10+ at 72 hpf.
claims.source: We found that similar to MEP glia in the periphery of control larvae, centrally located MEP glia in foxd3-/- larvae were Sox10+ at 72 hpf (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Foxd3 is detected first in 66.66% of MEP glia examined between 44 and 48 hpf.
claims.source: From our data, we observed that foxd3 was detected first in 66.66% of the cells we examined, while sox10 expression was detected first in 8.33% of the cells (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Sox10 expression was detected first in 8.33% of MEP glia examined between 44 and 48 hpf.
claims.source: From our data, we observed that foxd3 was detected first in 66.66% of the cells we examined, while sox10 expression was detected first in 8.33% of the cells (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: In 25% of MEP glia examined, foxd3 and sox10 were detected simultaneously.
claims.source: In 25% of the cells we analyzed, foxd3 and sox10 were detected simultaneously, likely because we did not detect the cells early enough in their development.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding with an interpretation.

claims.claim: Sox10 expression in MEP glia is subsequent to, but independent of, foxd3 expression.
claims.source: From this data, we conclude that sox10 expression in MEP glia is subsequent to, but independent of, foxd3 expression.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from time-lapse imaging data.

claims.claim: MEP glia are specified in foxd3-/- larvae.
claims.source: Taken together, we conclude that MEP glia are specified in foxd3-/- larvae.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claims.claim: In foxd3-/- larvae, MEP glia are located in the floor plate at 72 hpf and have a morphology reminiscent of radial glia.
claims.source: We found that while MEP glia were present along peripheral motor axons in heterozygous siblings, they were located in the floor plate in foxd3-/- larvae and had a morphology reminiscent of radial glia (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: MEP glia do not delaminate from the lateral floor plate in foxd3 mutants.
claims.source: We conclude from these observations that MEP glia do not delaminate from the lateral floor plate in foxd3 mutants.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from imaging observations.

claims.claim: Electroporation experiments in chick show that ectopic overexpression of foxd3 in the neural tube leads to the delamination of supernumerary neural crest like-cells.
claims.source: Electroporation experiments in chick show that ectopic overexpression of foxd3 in the neural tube leads to the delamination of supernumerary neural crest like-cells (Dottori et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: At 55 hpf, supernumerary nkx2.2+/foxd3+ MEP glia-like cells are observed in the CNS of foxd3 mRNA-injected embryos.
claims.source: At 55 hpf, we observed supernumerary nkx2.2+/foxd3+ MEP glia-like cells in the CNS of injected embryos (Figure 3H,I).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 3H,I.

claims.claim: A supernumerary MEP glial-like cell generated in the lateral floor plate of foxd3 mRNA-injected larvae eventually exits the spinal cord at MEP TZs.
claims.source: When we time-lapse imaged these larvae from 50 to 72 hpf, we observed that while a single MEP glial cell exited the control spinal cord (Video 3), a supernumerary MEP glial-like cell generated in the lateral floor plate of foxd3 mRNA-injected larvae eventually exited the spinal cord at MEP TZs (Video 4).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by time-lapse imaging data in Video 4.

claims.claim: MEP glia delaminate from the lateral floor plate of the spinal cord in a foxd3-dependent manner, analogous to neural crest cell foxd3-dependent delamination and migration.
claims.source: From these experiments, we conclude that MEP glia delaminate from the lateral floor plate of the spinal cord in a foxd3-dependent manner, analogous to neural crest cell foxd3-dependent delamination and migration (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data and comparison to neural crest cells.

claims.claim: The boundary between the CNS and PNS is composed of radial glial endfeet that secrete extracellular matrix components to establish a basal lamina.
claims.source: The boundary between the CNS and PNS is composed of radial glial endfeet that secrete extracellular matrix components to establish a basal lamina (Fraher et al., 2007; Lee and Song, 2013; Smith et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Cells secrete enzymes such as matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) to degrade proteins of the extracellular matrix in order to migrate through it.
claims.source: Cells, including neurons and their growth cones, secrete enzymes such as matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) to degrade proteins of the extracellular matrix in order to migrate through it (Hehr et al., 2005; McFarlane, 2003; Yong et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: At 48 hpf, nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia delaminate from the lateral floor plate and exit the spinal cord in DMSO-treated control larvae.
claims.source: At 48 hpf, we observed nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia delaminate from the lateral floor plate and exit the spinal cord in DMSO-treated control larvae (Figure 4A and Video 5).
claims.evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 4A and Video 5.

claims.claim: In GM6001-treated larvae, nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia delaminate from the lateral floor plate but stall at the edge of the CNS/PNS boundary and rarely exit into the periphery.
claims.source: In contrast, in GM6001-treated larvae, we detected delamination of nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia from the lateral floor plate, but they stalled at the edge of the CNS/PNS boundary and rarely exited into the periphery (Figure 4A and Video 6).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 4A and Video 6.

claims.claim: At 55 hpf, 90.61% of MEP glia exit the spinal cord in control larvae, while only 8.58% migrate out of the spinal cord when MMPs are inhibited, and 53.01% are stalled in the CNS.
claims.source: Quantification revealed that while 90.61% MEP glia exited the spinal cord in control larvae by 55 hpf, only 8.58% migrated out of the spinal cord when MMPs were inhibited, and 53.01% were stalled in the CNS (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: By 72 hpf, 100% of MEP glia are found in the PNS of control larvae, whereas 46.65% are located in the spinal cord of GM6001-treated larvae and only 31.78% are present along spinal motor nerves.
claims.source: By 72 hpf, 100% of MEP glia were found in the PNS of control larvae, whereas 46.65% were located in the spinal cord of GM6001-treated larvae and only 31.78% were present along spinal motor nerves (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Foxd3+/nkx2.2a+ MEP glia are observed stalled in the CNS of GM6001-treated larvae at 72 hpf, in a position adjacent to the midline.
claims.source: In contrast, we often observed foxd3+/nkx2.2a+ MEP glia stalled in the CNS of GM6001-treated larvae at 72 hpf, in a position adjacent to the midline (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Blocking MMPs inhibits MEP glial migration out of the spinal cord and phenocopies the foxd3 mutant phenotype.
claims.source: From these results, we conclude that blocking MMPs inhibits MEP glial migration out of the spinal cord and phenocopies the foxd3 mutant phenotype.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data.

claims.claim: Mmp17b and adamts3 are expressed in the ventral neural tube at 48 hpf, prior to MEP glial exit.
claims.source: From these studies, we found that mmp17b and adamts3 were expressed in the ventral neural tube at 48 hpf, prior to MEP glial exit (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: In foxd3-/- embryos, expression of mmp17b is unchanged in the spinal cord at 48 hpf.
claims.source: In foxd3-/- embryos, we observed that while expression of mmp17b was unchanged in the spinal cord, adamts3 expression was significantly reduced in the ventral neural tube at 48 hpf (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: In foxd3-/- embryos, adamts3 expression is significantly reduced in the ventral neural tube at 48 hpf.
claims.source: In foxd3-/- embryos, we observed that while expression of mmp17b was unchanged in the spinal cord, adamts3 expression was significantly reduced in the ventral neural tube at 48 hpf (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: No change in adamts3 expression is observed in the spinal cord of embryos overexpressing foxd3.
claims.source: However, we did not observe any change in adamts3 expression in the spinal cord of embryos overexpressing foxd3 (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary observation supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Overexpression of human adamTS3 mRNA does not result in more MEP glial delamination from the precursor domain.
claims.source: Reciprocally, overexpression of human adamTS3 mRNA did not result in more MEP glial delamination from the precursor domain (control: mean ± SEM = 1.06 ± 0.056, n = 18 nerves from five embryos; adamts3 mRNA: mean ± SEM = 1 ± 0.00, n = 29 nerves from nine embryos; p=0.38).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantitative data.

claims.claim: One MEP glial cell per somite is observed stalled inside the spinal cord in foxd3 mutants, just medial to the MEP TZ, in a repetitive pattern along the anterior-posterior axis of the neural tube.
claims.source: In our foxd3 mutant analysis, we always observed the presence of one MEP glial cell per somite, stalled inside the spinal cord, just medial to the MEP TZ, in a repetitive pattern along the anterior-posterior axis of the neural tube (Figure 3A,E and F).
claims.evidence: This is a consistent observation supported by imaging data in Figure 3A,E,F.

claims.claim: Time-lapse movies consistently show one cell exiting the spinal cord at MEP TZs and dividing in the periphery in control embryos.
claims.source: Additionally, our time-lapse movies consistently showed one cell exiting the spinal cord at MEP TZs and dividing in the periphery in control embryos (Video 7).
claims.evidence: This is a consistent observation supported by time-lapse imaging data in Video 7.

claims.claim: Radial glial precursors give rise to a single MEP glial cell progenitor per hemi-segment.
claims.source: This led us to hypothesize that radial glial precursors give rise to a single MEP glial cell progenitor per hemi-segment.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on observations.

claims.claim: 96.67% of MEP glia present along a single motor nerve are the same color in nkx2.2a:cre;ubi:zebrabow larvae at 4 dpf, indicating they originated from the same nkx2.2a+ precursor.
claims.source: When we looked at the color profile of 214 nkx2.2a+/Sox10+ MEP glia along 60 motor nerves at 4 dpf in confocal z-stack images, we found that 96.67% of MEP glia present along a single motor nerve were the same color, and therefore, originated from the same nkx2.2a+ precursor (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by lineage tracing data in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The color profiles of MEP glia present along the same motor nerve cluster together, while fluorescent profiles of MEP glia present along distinct nerves segregate.
claims.source: Using a ternary plot, we observed that the color profiles of MEP glia that were present along the same motor nerve always clustered together (yellow dots cluster together, pink dots cluster together, and white dots cluster together), while fluorescent profiles of MEP glia present along distinct nerves segregated, indicating that MEP glia along the same nerve share a common progenitor, and that each hemi-segment has a single, unique MEP glial progenitor (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantitative analysis in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: MEP glia along the same nerve share a common progenitor, and each hemi-segment has a single, unique MEP glial progenitor.
claims.source: Using a ternary plot, we observed that the color profiles of MEP glia that were present along the same motor nerve always clustered together (yellow dots cluster together, pink dots cluster together, and white dots cluster together), while fluorescent profiles of MEP glia present along distinct nerves segregated, indicating that MEP glia along the same nerve share a common progenitor, and that each hemi-segment has a single, unique MEP glial progenitor (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from lineage tracing data.

claims.claim: 74% of MEP glia imaged at 72 hpf were EdU+ and therefore proliferated between 50 and 56 hpf.
claims.source: We found that 74% of the MEP glia we imaged at 72 hpf were EdU+ and therefore, proliferated between 50 and 56 hpf.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by EdU incorporation assay data.

claims.claim: 1 to 4 MEP glial cell divisions are observed along motor nerve axons between 48 and 72 hpf.
claims.source: We also quantified MEP glial cell division in our time-lapse movies between 48 and 72 hpf and observed 1 to 4 MEP glial cell divisions along motor nerve axons (Figure 5D), which generated up to six cells per nerve by 4 dpf (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: MEP glia populate motor nerve roots by undergoing cell division.
claims.source: From these studies we conclude that MEP glia populate motor nerve roots by undergoing cell division.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from proliferation assay and time-lapse imaging data.

claims.claim: At 72 hpf, only one MEP glial cell per hemi-segment is observed along motor nerve roots in aphidicolin and HUA-treated larvae.
claims.source: When we imaged larvae at 72 hpf, we detected several MEP glia per motor nerve in DMSO-treated larvae, but only saw one MEP glial cell per hemi-segment along motor nerve roots in aphidicolin and HUA-treated larvae (Figure 5E,F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 5E,F.

claims.claim: CNS precursors give rise to a single MEP glial progenitor cell per hemi-segment in the neural tube, and this cell exits the CNS and acts as a progenitor that further divides to give rise to all MEP glia found on a single motor nerve.
claims.source: This data supports our hypothesis that CNS precursors give rise to a single MEP glial progenitor cell per hemi-segment in the neural tube, and that this cell exits the CNS and acts as a progenitor that further divides to give rise to all MEP glia found on a single motor nerve.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from cell cycle arrest experiments.

claims.claim: Foxd3+/sox2+ MEP glia are detected in the PNS at 52 hpf and as late as 5 dpf.
claims.source: We imaged sox2:egfp;foxd3:mcherry embryos and larvae and detected foxd3+/sox2+ MEP glia in the PNS at 52 hpf (Figure 5G) and as late as 5 dpf (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), revealing that some MEP glia maintain a progenitor state.
claims.evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Some MEP glia maintain a progenitor state.
claims.source: We imaged sox2:egfp;foxd3:mcherry embryos and larvae and detected foxd3+/sox2+ MEP glia in the PNS at 52 hpf (Figure 5G) and as late as 5 dpf (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), revealing that some MEP glia maintain a progenitor state.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from imaging data showing sox2 expression.

claims.claim: BLBP+/nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia are observed along motor nerve root axons at 55 hpf.
claims.source: In these larvae, we observed BLBP+/nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia along motor nerve root axons at 55 hpf (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: MEP glia along the same nerve come from a single progenitor and divide several times to populate spinal motor nerve root axons.
claims.source: Together, these results show that MEP glia along the same nerve come from a single progenitor and divide several times to populate spinal motor nerve root axons.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claims.claim: Interactions with axons are essential for Schwann cell migration, development, and function.
claims.source: Because they reside along the same axons as Schwann cells, and because interactions with axons are essential for Schwann cell migration, development, and function (Fontenas et al., 2016; Gilmour et al., 2002; Lyons et al., 2005; Miyamoto et al., 2017; Perlin et al., 2011; Voas et al., 2007), we hypothesized that MEP glial development also depends on axonal cues.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: PlexinA3 mutants are characterized by intraspinal motor axon guidance defects that result in ectopic, supernumerary MEP TZs where motor axons ectopically exit into the periphery.
claims.source: PlexinA3 mutants are characterized by intraspinal motor axon guidance defects that result in ectopic, supernumerary MEP TZs where motor axons ectopically exit into the periphery.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about plexinA3 mutants.

claims.claim: MEP glia are present along every motor nerve, including ectopic ones, in both plexina3 mutant and WT larvae.
claims.source: We then imaged photoconverted plexina3;nbt:dsred;sox10:eos mutant and WT siblings from 48 to 72 hpf and observed the presence of MEP glia along every motor nerve, including ectopic ones, in both mutant and WT larvae (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B.

claims.claim: Motor axons are sufficient to induce MEP glial migration into the periphery.
claims.source: From this data, we conclude that motor axons are sufficient to induce MEP glial migration into the periphery.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from plexinA3 mutant analysis.

claims.claim: In MTZ-treated hb9:yfp-ntr larvae, MEP glia do not exit the spinal cord at MEP TZs where motor nerves are genetically ablated.
claims.source: In these studies, we did not detect any MEP glial migration out of the spinal cord at MEP TZs where motor nerves were genetically ablated (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: In MTZ-treated hb9:yfp-ntr larvae, OPCs in the spinal cord and Schwann cells along sensory nerves both develop and migrate normally.
claims.source: In these time-lapse movies, OPCs in the spinal cord and Schwann cells along sensory nerves both developed and migrated normally.
claims.evidence: This is a primary observation from time-lapse imaging.

claims.claim: At 72 hpf, wif1+ MEP glia are detected along motor roots in control larvae, but only inside the spinal cord of MTZ-treated hb9:yfp-ntr larvae.
claims.source: At 72 hpf, we detected wif1+ MEP glia along motor roots in control larvae (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A). In contrast, we only observed wif1 expression inside the spinal cord of MTZ-treated hb9:yfp-ntr larvae (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Foxd3+ peripheral MEP glia are observed along motor axons in control larvae at 50 and 72 hpf, but only spinal cord-located foxd3+ MEP glia are observed in MTZ-treated larvae.
claims.source: While we saw foxd3+ peripheral MEP glia along motor axons in control larvae, we only saw spinal cord-located foxd3+ MEP glia in MTZ-treated larvae at both 50 and 72 hpf and did not see any along degenerating motor axons (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Spinal motor axons are necessary and sufficient to drive MEP glial migration into the PNS.
claims.source: We conclude from these experiments that spinal motor axons are necessary and sufficient to drive MEP glial migration into the PNS.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from motor neuron ablation and plexinA3 mutant experiments.

claims.claim: Axonally-derived Neuregulin1 type III is essential for many aspects of Schwann cell development, including directed migration, proliferation, and myelination along motor axons.

results.result: MEP glia originate from nkx2.2a+/olig2+ radial glial precursors in the lateral floor plate of the spinal cord. These precursors express both CNS markers (nkx2.2a, olig2) and PNS markers (foxd3, sox10), and maintain expression of both marker types once in the PNS. The cells have morphology and position reminiscent of radial glia and express GFAP.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C24, C25, C41, C43, C48, C57-C64 are supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including live imaging (Figure 1B-F, Figure 2A-C), marker expression analysis (Figure 1G-I), immunohistochemistry (Figure 2D), and in situ hybridization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D). The identification of nkx2.2a as a new marker for MEP glia is well-documented through imaging at multiple developmental stages. The conclusion that MEP glia originate from lateral floor plate nkx2.2a+/olig2+ radial glial precursors is supported by co-expression analysis and morphological observations.

results.result: Foxd3 is required for MEP glia to delaminate from the lateral floor plate and exit the spinal cord. In foxd3-/- larvae, MEP glia are specified and express Sox10 but remain in the ventral spinal cord and fail to migrate into the periphery. Foxd3 expression precedes Sox10 expression in MEP glia, and Sox10 expression is independent of foxd3. MEP glia delaminate in a foxd3-dependent manner analogous to neural crest cell delamination.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C25, C65-C88 are strongly supported by time-lapse imaging (Figure 3A, Videos 1-2), quantitative analysis (Figure 3C-D), in situ hybridization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), immunohistochemistry (Figure 3F), and temporal expression analysis (Figure 3G). The foxd3 mutant phenotype is well-characterized showing MEP glia specification occurs but delamination and exit fail. The conclusion that foxd3 is required for delamination but not specification is supported by multiple independent assays including wif1 expression and Sox10 immunostaining.

results.result: Overexpression of foxd3 is sufficient to generate supernumerary MEP glia-like cells in the CNS that eventually exit the spinal cord at MEP TZs. This demonstrates that foxd3 can induce delamination of MEP glia from the lateral floor plate.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C88 are supported by foxd3 mRNA injection experiments with imaging data (Figure 3H-I) and time-lapse imaging (Video 4). The observation of supernumerary nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ cells in the CNS that exit through MEP TZs provides gain-of-function evidence complementing the loss-of-function foxd3 mutant data. The analogy to neural crest cell delamination is supported by citation to previous work in chick (C85).

results.result: MEP glial exit from the spinal cord requires matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs). Inhibition of MMPs with GM6001 prevents MEP glia from crossing the CNS/PNS boundary, phenocopying the foxd3 mutant. Mmp17b and adamts3 are expressed in the ventral neural tube prior to MEP glial exit, and adamts3 expression is reduced in foxd3-/- embryos.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C101 are supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments (Figure 4A-D, Videos 5-6), quantitative analysis (Figure 4B-C), and in situ hybridization (Figure 4E). The GM6001 treatment experiments show that MMP inhibition blocks MEP glial migration out of the spinal cord with quantitative data showing 90.61% exit in controls vs 8.58% in treated embryos at 55 hpf. The identification of adamts3 as a potential downstream target of foxd3 is supported by expression analysis, though the lack of effect of adamts3 overexpression (C101) suggests additional factors are involved.

results.result: Neural tube precursors give rise to a single MEP glial progenitor cell per hemi-segment that exits the CNS and divides to populate motor nerve roots. Lineage tracing using Zebrabow shows 96.67% of MEP glia along a single motor nerve originated from the same nkx2.2a+ precursor. MEP glia proliferate between 50-56 hpf (74% EdU+) and undergo 1-4 cell divisions to generate up to 6 cells per nerve by 4 dpf. Some MEP glia maintain progenitor markers (sox2, BLBP).
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C116 are supported by multiple lines of evidence including lineage tracing (Figure 5A-C), EdU incorporation assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C), time-lapse imaging quantification (Figure 5D), cell cycle arrest experiments (Figure 5E-F), and progenitor marker expression (Figure 5G-H). The Zebrabow clonal analysis provides strong evidence that MEP glia along the same nerve share a common progenitor (96.67% same color). The cell cycle arrest experiments showing only one MEP glia per hemi-segment when proliferation is blocked (Figure 5E-F) directly support the single progenitor model.

results.result: Spinal motor axons are necessary and sufficient to drive MEP glial migration into the PNS. In plexinA3 mutants with ectopic motor exit points, MEP glia are present along all motor nerves including ectopic ones. When motor neurons are genetically ablated using hb9:yfp-ntr and metronidazole, MEP glia fail to exit the spinal cord but are specified (wif1+ cells remain in CNS).
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C125 are supported by experiments in plexinA3 mutants (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B) and motor neuron ablation experiments (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-B). The presence of MEP glia along ectopic motor nerves in plexinA3 mutants demonstrates sufficiency of motor axons. The motor neuron ablation experiments showing MEP glia remain in the CNS (wif1+ and foxd3+ cells detected in spinal cord but not PNS) demonstrate necessity of motor axons. Controls showing normal OPC and Schwann cell development rule out non-specific effects.

results.result: Neuregulin1 type III (nrg1) expressed on motor axons drives MEP glial migration to motor roots. In nrg1-/- and erbb3b mutants, MEP glia and Schwann cells are absent from motor nerve roots. MEP glia exit the spinal cord in nrg1 mutants but fail to associate with motor root axons and migrate away (wif1+ cells found distally near lateral line nerve). OPC processes extend into the PNS in nrg1 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C140 are supported by analysis of nrg1-/- and erbb3b mutants using photoconversion (Figure 7A), in situ hybridization (Figure 7B-C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B), and citations to previous work. The observation that MEP glia exit the spinal cord but migrate away from motor roots in nrg1 mutants (wif1+ cells found distally) demonstrates nrg1 is required for directed migration rather than exit per se. The similar phenotype in erbb3b mutants supports the conclusion that nrg1 signals through erbb3b receptors.

results.result: Overexpression of neuregulin1 type III in CNS neurons is sufficient to generate additional MEP glia from nkx2.2a+ radial glial precursors in the post-embryonic spinal cord. Nrg1 overexpression increases proliferation of ventral spinal cord PH3+/nkx2.2a+ cells and increases the total number of MEP glia along motor nerves. Sox2+/nkx2.2a+ radial glial progenitors persist in the spinal cord at 4 dpf, suggesting nrg1 can control their proliferation.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C150 are supported by neuregulin overexpression experiments using neuroD:gal4;UAS:hNrg1 larvae with in situ hybridization (Figure 8A), live imaging (Figure 8B-C), immunohistochemistry (Figure 8D-F), and EdU incorporation assays (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B-C). The observation of additional nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia in the ventral spinal cord (Figure 8B-C) and increased PH3+/nkx2.2a+ proliferating cells (Figure 8D-E) supports the conclusion that nrg1 regulates MEP glial progenitor proliferation. The detection of Sox2+/nkx2.2a+ cells at 4 dpf (Figure 8F) supports the conclusion that radial glial precursors persist in post-embryonic development.

results.result: Ventral spinal cord precursors employ neural crest cell (NCC) developmental mechanisms to generate hybrid, peripheral myelinating glia.
results.evaluation: Claim C29 is a high-level conclusion supported by the collective evidence from multiple experiments. The use of foxd3 for delamination (analogous to NCCs), requirement for MMPs for migration through the CNS/PNS boundary, dependence on axonal neuregulin signaling (similar to Schwann cells), and expression of both CNS and PNS markers all support this conclusion. This represents an integration of the major findings rather than a single experimental result.

results.result: MEP glia transiently express olig2 until approximately 55 hpf with dramatically diminished GFP fluorescence after exiting the spinal cord. Olig2-driven eGFP levels in MEP glia are 4.18 times lower than pMN domain cells and 7.68 times lower than OPCs at 55 hpf. In situ hybridization shows no olig2+ cell bodies in the PNS at 48 or 72 hpf. In contrast, nkx2.2a-driven GFP fluorescence remains stable after MEP glial exit. The olig2 pMN domain and nkx2.2a lateral floor plate merge to form a mixed domain by 48 hpf.
results.evaluation: Claims C44, C49-C56 are supported by quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements (Figure 1G-I), time course analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C), in situ hybridization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and imaging of neural tube sections (Figure 1—figure supplement 3). The quantitative data clearly show differential regulation of olig2 vs nkx2.2a expression in MEP glia. The observation that the pMN and lateral floor plate domains merge by 48 hpf is consistent with previous literature on OPC specification.

results.result: Background and context claims establishing the known biology of oligodendrocytes, Schwann cells, MEP glia, neural tube organization, and the knowledge gaps addressed by the study.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C7-C23, C30-C40 are primarily background knowledge claims supported by citations to previous literature. These establish the context for the study including: (1) the known functions of oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells, (2) the previous identification of MEP glia by the authors, (3) the organization of the neural tube, (4) the knowledge gaps regarding MEP glial origin and development. These claims are well-supported by appropriate citations and provide necessary context for interpreting the new findings.

results.result: At 72 hpf and 4 dpf, both nkx2.2a+/sox10+ MEP glia and nkx2.2a+/sox10- perineurial glia are observed along motor nerve axons. MEP glial membrane sheaths are reminiscent of myelin internodes, while perineurial cell membranes are loose. Mbp+ myelin sheaths are formed by foxd3+ cells along motor root axons at 4 dpf.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are supported by imaging data (Figure 1D-F) showing the morphological and molecular distinctions between MEP glia and perineurial glia. The observations are consistent with previous characterization of these cell types and provide additional marker information (nkx2.2a) to distinguish them.

results.result: One foxd3+ cell is consistently detected in the ventral spinal cord per hemi-segment of the zebrafish trunk.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 is supported by consistent observations across multiple imaging experiments (Figure 1B, Figure 2A-B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1). This observation is important for establishing the single progenitor model but is a descriptive finding rather than a mechanistic result.
